entries.title: 🧱 malloc - how it works
entries.content:
malloc() allocates a block of memory on the heap and returns a void pointer to it.
You must cast it and free it manually - C won't do it for you.

Syntax:
```
void *malloc(size_t size);
```

Example - allocate an array of 10 ints:
```
int *arr = (int *)malloc(10 * sizeof(int));
if (arr == NULL)
    return (1); // always check for NULL!
arr[0] = 42;
free(arr);
```

Common mistakes:
- Forgetting to check if malloc returned NULL
- Forgetting to free() - causes memory leaks
- Freeing twice (double free) - undefined behaviour
- Off-by-one: malloc(len) for a string needs to be malloc(len + 1) for the '\0'
tips: Always check for NULL after malloc()
sizeof(type) keeps your code portable
Use valgrind to detect memory leaks

entries.title: 📌 Pointers - basics
entries.content:
A pointer stores the memory address of a variable.

```
int x = 42;
int *p = &x;   // p holds the address of x
printf("%d\n", *p); // dereference: prints 42
*p = 100;          // modifies x through the pointer
```

Pointer arithmetic:
```
int arr[3] = {1, 2, 3};
int *p = arr;   // points to arr[0]
p++;            // now points to arr[1]
printf("%d\n", *p); // 2
```
tips: & gives you the address of a variable
* on a pointer gives you the value at that address
Arrays decay into pointers to their first element

entries.title: 📝 Strings in C
tips: Always allocate strlen + 1 for the null terminator
String literals are read-only - never write to them
ft_strlen loops until it hits '\0'

entries.title: 🖨️ write() - printing without printf
tips: At 42, printf may be forbidden - learn write()
write() doesn't add a newline - you must add '\n' yourself
Return value is the number of bytes written, or -1 on error

entries.title: 🗂️ Structs
tips: Use typedef to avoid writing 'struct' everywhere
-> is arrow notation for pointer-to-struct member access
42 style: struct names start with s_, typedef names with t_

entries.title: 🔗 Linked lists
tips: Always check malloc return before using the node
The last node's ->next is NULL - use this to detect end
To free: traverse and free each node, don't free head first

entries.title: ⚙️ Preprocessor - macros & header guards
entries.content:
The C preprocessor runs before compilation. It handles #include, #define, and conditionals.

Header guard - prevents a header being included twice:
```
#ifndef MY_HEADER_H
# define MY_HEADER_H

// your declarations here

#endif
```

Simple macro:
```
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

int x = MAX(3, 7); // expands to ((3) > (7) ? (3) : (7))
```

Debug macro - prints only when DEBUG is defined:
```
#ifdef DEBUG
# define LOG(msg) fprintf(stderr, "[DBG] %s\n", msg)
#else
# define LOG(msg)
#endif
```

Compile with debug:
```
gcc -DDEBUG -o prog prog.c
```
tips: Always wrap macro arguments in () to avoid operator precedence bugs
Header guards stop circular includes from breaking your build
#ifndef vs #pragma once - 42 style uses #ifndef

entries.title: 🎯 Function Pointers - callbacks & simulated OOP
tips: Read the type right-to-left: int (*fp)(int) = 'fp is a pointer to a function taking int returning int'
Use typedef to make function pointer types readable
This is exactly how ft_list_foreach and ft_list_remove_if work!

entries.title: 🌐 Static vs Global - scope control
tips: static local: same as global lifetime, function scope - great for GNL
static global: hides variable from other .c files (encapsulation)
42 norm: global vars must start with g_

entries.title: 🔧 FDs & Pipes - dup2, pipe, and redirection
tips: Always close the end of the pipe you're not using - or read() will block forever
dup2(new, old) replaces 'old' with a copy of 'new'
This is the core of pipex and minishell!

entries.title: 🏗️ Stack vs Heap - memory layout
entries.content:
C programs have two main memory regions:

STACK - automatic, fast, limited:
```
void foo(void)
{
    int x = 42;      // lives on the stack
    char buf[256];   // also stack
}                    // x and buf die here!
```

HEAP - manual, slower, as big as RAM allows:
```
char *s = malloc(256); // lives on heap until free()
// s survives after the function returns
```

realloc() - resize a heap allocation:
```
int *arr = malloc(5 * sizeof(int));
// ... arr grows ...
arr = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int)); // now 10 ints
if (!arr) // realloc can return NULL!
    return (1);
```

Danger - returning a pointer to a stack variable:
```
char *bad(void)
{
    char buf[10] = "hello"; // stack!
    return buf;  // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR - stack freed on return
}
```
tips: Stack overflows happen with very deep recursion or huge local arrays
realloc may move the memory - always reassign the pointer
Rule of thumb: if it needs to outlive the function, heap it

entries.title: ⌨️ argc & argv - reading the command line
tips: Read the argument rule twice: 'one argument' means argc == 2, not 1
Subjects are exact about what to print on the wrong argc - usually just '\n'
argv strings are writable, so in-place transforms are allowed

entries.title: 🔩 Bitwise operations - masks and shifts
tips: rank02: print_bits, swap_bits, reverse_bits, is_power_of_2
Use unsigned types - >> on a negative signed int copies the sign bit
(x >> i) & 1 reads bit i; x |= (1 << i) sets it; x &= ~(1 << i) clears it

entries.title: 🌲 Recursion & backtracking - choose, explore, un-choose
tips: rank03 n_queens, permutations, powerset, rip and tsp are ALL this pattern
Forgetting the un-choose step is the single most common bug
Write the base case before the loop or you will recurse forever
For permutations, swap element i with each later element, recurse, swap back

entries.title: 🍴 fork, exec & wait - the process model
tips: rank04 ft_popen, picoshell - see also 'FDs & Pipes' for the plumbing
Unclosed write ends are why a pipeline hangs forever instead of finishing
exec only returns on failure, so treat 'it returned' as the error branch
Wait for ALL children before returning, not just the last one

entries.title: 🚨 Signals & alarm - timeouts and crash detection
tips: rank04 sandbox must distinguish clean exit, bad exit, crash and timeout
WIFEXITED and WIFSIGNALED are how you tell 'returned 1' from 'segfaulted'
alarm(0) cancels a pending alarm - do that once the child is reaped
Do not call printf inside a handler; set a flag and print outside

entries.title: 📖 read() & static buffers - the get_next_line shape
entries.content:
```
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, BUFFER_SIZE);
```
  n > 0   bytes read
  n == 0  end of file
  n < 0   error

read() does NOT null-terminate. You must write `buf[n] = '\0'` yourself,
which is why the buffer is declared one byte bigger than BUFFER_SIZE.

A `static` variable inside a function keeps its value between calls -
that is how get_next_line remembers the leftovers of the last read:
```
char *get_next_line(int fd)
{
    static char stash[BUFFER_SIZE + 1];
    /* ... */
    return (0);
}
```

The usual loop: if the stash already holds a newline, cut the line out of
it and keep the rest. Otherwise read more and append, until you find a
newline or hit EOF.
tips: rank03 broken_gnl - the bug is nearly always in the leftover handling
Test: last line with no trailing newline, empty file, and a line longer than BUFFER_SIZE
Check n == 0 and n < 0 separately - treating -1 as EOF hides real errors
A static buffer is per-fd state; reading two fds at once breaks a naive version

entries.title: 🔍 Recursive descent - parsing by grammar
tips: rank04 vbc (arithmetic) and argo (JSON) are both exactly this
Write the grammar as a comment first - the code then writes itself
The error message usually must name the offending character, so keep the cursor exact
Check for leftover input after the top-level rule: '1+2)' must be an error

entries.title: 🗺️ 2D grids in C - allocation and traversal
tips: rank05 bsq and life
A flat buffer is one malloc and one free - far fewer ways to leak
Bound-check BEFORE indexing; C will happily read off the end of the array
With char **, free every row and then the row array, in that order
